learn.hook: Parliament passes a law guaranteeing rural jobs. But who actually opens the worksites, pays the wages and checks the muster rolls? That's the executive.
points: The executive is the organ of government that implements laws and policies and runs the day-to-day administration.

Political executive: elected leaders (PM, ministers, Chief Ministers) who make policy and change with elections. Permanent executive: civil servants who carry out policy and stay in office regardless of elections.
Presidential system: the President is head of both state and government, usually directly elected, and not responsible to the legislature for survival (e.g. USA, Brazil, most of Latin America).

Parliamentary system: the Prime Minister and cabinet are the real executive and are responsible to the legislature; the head of state (a President or monarch) is mostly nominal (e.g. UK, India, Germany, Italy, Japan, Portugal).

Semi-presidential system: a powerful President and a Prime Minister with a council of ministers share power; the President may belong to a different party from the PM (e.g. France, Russia, Sri Lanka).

example.q: Classify the executive: (a) a head of state and government directly elected for a fixed term who chooses ministers from outside the legislature; (b) a PM who stays in office only while the lower house supports her; (c) a directly elected President who appoints a PM responsible to parliament.
steps: (a) Head of state = head of government, not dependent on legislature → presidential.
(b) Real executive depends on legislature's confidence → parliamentary.
(c) Strong President plus a PM answerable to parliament → semi-presidential.

learn.reallife: When a new government takes office after the Lok Sabha elections, ministers change but the District Collector keeps running the district — political executive changes, permanent executive stays.

teach.praise: Hoot! Presidential, parliamentary, semi-presidential — and political versus permanent executive. Gappu is now a constitution nerd!
teach.nudge: Which type of executive is answerable to the legislature?

learn.hook: The President of India is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces, signs every law and appoints the Prime Minister — yet is called a 'nominal' head. How can both be true?
points: The Constitution makers chose the parliamentary system because India had experience of it under British rule, it keeps the executive accountable to elected representatives, and it avoids a personality cult around a single all-powerful leader.
The President is the formal head of the state; real executive power is exercised by the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.
The President is elected indirectly by an electoral college of elected MPs (both Houses) and elected MLAs of the States, using the Single Transferable Vote. A candidate must be at least 35.
Term: five years. The President can be removed only by impeachment for 'violation of the Constitution', which needs a resolution passed by two-thirds of the total membership of each House.
Because the President is not directly elected, no President can claim a personal popular mandate against the elected government.

example.q: Why might the makers have avoided a directly elected President for India?
steps: A directly elected President could claim a popular mandate equal to or greater than the PM's.
This could create two rival centres of power.
An indirectly elected, nominal President keeps real power with the ministry responsible to the Lok Sabha.
example.answer: To avoid rival power centres and keep power with the accountable ministry.

learn.reallife: On Republic Day, the President takes the salute at Kartavya Path as Supreme Commander, but the decision to deploy troops is taken by the Union Cabinet — nominal head, real executive.

options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Both true; indirect election is why the President lacks a separate direct mandate.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the mode of election to the President's role

quiz.explain: STV is used for the President's election.

teach.praise: Great! Indirectly elected, nominal head, real power with the PM-led ministry, and impeachment for violating the Constitution!
teach.nudge: Who actually uses the President's powers in day-to-day governance?

learn.hook: In 1986 a President simply sat on a bill and never signed it. No deadline in the Constitution forced him to act. Welcome to the 'pocket veto'.
points: Formal powers: executive (all executive actions in the President's name), legislative (summoning Parliament, assent to bills), financial (money bills introduced on recommendation), military (Supreme Commander) and diplomatic (treaties, ambassadors). All are exercised on ministers' advice.

Article 74(1): the President shall act in accordance with the advice of the Council of Ministers; the President may ask the Council to reconsider its advice once, but must act on the advice given after reconsideration.
Discretion 1: the right to be informed of all important matters and decisions of the Council of Ministers; the PM must communicate them.

Discretion 2: the President can return a bill (other than a money bill) for reconsideration; if Parliament passes it again, the President must sign. Since no time limit is fixed, the President can keep a bill pending indefinitely — a 'pocket veto', as with the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill in 1986.
Discretion 3: choosing the PM when no party or coalition has a clear majority in the Lok Sabha, as in hung parliaments after 1989.

example.q: Parliament sends the President a non-money bill. Trace what she can do and what follows.
steps: She may sign it — it becomes law.
She may return it once for reconsideration.
If Parliament passes it again (with or without changes), she must give assent.
She may also simply not act on it for a long time — a pocket veto, since no time limit is fixed.
example.answer: Sign, return once (then must sign), or delay indefinitely (pocket veto). For a money bill she cannot return it.

learn.reallife: After an election with no clear winner, all eyes turn to Rashtrapati Bhavan: the President's choice of whom to invite first can shape the next government.

learn.hook: A government with 300 ministers? Not allowed. Since 2003 the Constitution caps the size of the ministry, after years of jumbo cabinets formed to keep allies happy.
points: The Vice-President is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament (STV), holds office for five years, is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and acts as President when the office falls vacant until a new President is elected.
The Prime Minister must have the support of a majority in the Lok Sabha. The President appoints as PM the person who commands this majority.
A person who is not a member of Parliament can become PM or a minister, but must become a member of either House within six months.
The PM chooses ministers and allocates portfolios. The 91st Amendment (2003) limits the Council of Ministers to 15% of the total membership of the Lok Sabha (or of the Assembly, in States).
Collective responsibility: the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, the entire ministry must resign.

example.q: The Lok Sabha has 543 members. What is the maximum size of the Union Council of Ministers, including the PM?
steps: The 91st Amendment caps it at 15% of the total Lok Sabha membership.
Ministers must be whole persons and cannot exceed 15%, so the maximum is 81.

learn.reallife: Whenever a new ministry is sworn in at Rashtrapati Bhavan, analysts count heads to check it stays within the 15% cap of the 91st Amendment.

topics.title: Ministers, coalitions and the State executive

learn.hook: Between 1989 and 2014, no single party won a Lok Sabha majority on its own. Prime Ministers had to run governments like captains of a team of many clubs.
points: The Council of Ministers has three ranks: Cabinet Ministers (senior leaders in charge of major ministries who form the Cabinet), Ministers of State (in charge of smaller ministries or assisting Cabinet ministers; some hold independent charge) and Deputy Ministers (assist ministers).
The Cabinet, the inner circle led by the PM, takes the main decisions; collective responsibility binds all ministers to support Cabinet decisions in public.
In coalition governments, the PM's power to choose ministers and set policy is limited by allies' demands; decisions need consultation and compromise.
With a single-party majority, the PM's dominance over the Cabinet and party tends to increase.
State executive: the Governor is appointed by the President and is the nominal head; the Chief Minister, who leads the majority in the Assembly, heads the Council of Ministers, the real executive.

example.q: Compare the PM's power in a single-party majority government and in a coalition government.
steps: Single-party majority: the PM chooses ministers freely and leads a disciplined party.
Coalition: allies demand ministries and influence policy; the PM must negotiate.
So coalition politics generally reduces the PM's freedom of action.
example.answer: The PM is more dominant with a single-party majority; coalition politics limits the PM's power.

learn.reallife: When a state's Chief Minister presents the budget in the Vidhan Sabha while the Governor's address opens the session, you see real and nominal executive side by side.

options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

learn.hook: Ministers come and go, but the officers who run the railways, collect taxes and manage floods stay on. India's bureaucracy is one of the largest permanent workforces in the world.
points: The bureaucracy (civil service) is the permanent executive: trained and skilled officers who help ministers frame policy and implement it.
Civil servants are expected to be politically neutral: they serve whichever government is elected, without taking sides.

All India Services (e.g. IAS, IPS) are recruited by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and serve in States; there are also central services and State services (recruited by State Public Service Commissions).
Reservations in recruitment for SC, ST and OBC make the bureaucracy more representative of society.
Criticisms: red tape, insensitivity to ordinary citizens, and political interference (transfers, pressure). The Right to Information Act (2005) helps citizens hold officials accountable.

example.q: Raju applies for a ration card and hears nothing for months. What can he do under the Right to Information Act?
steps: File an RTI application asking the status of his application and the reasons for delay.
The office must reply within the time limit set by the Act.
This puts pressure on officials and exposes red tape.
example.answer: He can use RTI to seek information, making officials accountable.

learn.reallife: Every year lakhs of aspirants sit for the UPSC Civil Services Examination; those selected for the IAS or IPS may later serve as District Collectors or Superintendents of Police in any State.

teach.nudge: If ministers change every five years, who keeps the administration running?
